title: Passing the Test Isn't Proof: Why a 'Significant' Finding Can Still Be Wrong
audience: A curious adult with no background in this field

source.title: Why Most Published Research Findings Are False

intro.summary: The paper asks a simple question: when a study reports a 'statistically significant' finding, how likely is that finding to be true? Ioannidis builds a counting model. It combines the share of tested ideas that are really true, the study's chance of detecting a real effect (power), the usual 5% false-alarm rate, bias, and how many teams test the same question. Plugging in plausible values, he argues that in many fields a claimed finding is more likely false than true, and that small studies, small effects, many loosely chosen hypotheses, flexible analyses, conflicts of interest and crowded 'hot' fields all make this worse. The main limitation is that this is a theoretical model, not a measurement: its conclusions depend on assumed values for things like the pre-study odds and bias, which are hard to know for any real field.
background: Many studies declare a result 'statistically significant' when the p-value is below 0.05, which roughly means the data would be fairly surprising if there were no real effect.
Even when nothing real is going on, about 1 test in 20 will cross that 0.05 line by chance: a false alarm.
A study's 'power' is its chance of detecting an effect that really exists; small studies and small effects mean low power.
The same logic appears in medical screening: a positive test for a rare disease is often a false positive, because healthy people far outnumber sick ones.
intro.aha: In the paper's genome example, even with no bias at all, if ten teams test the same gene and one gets a significant result, the chance that gene is truly linked to the disease is barely higher than before anyone looked.

primer.heading: The question
primer.body: Published findings are sometimes overturned by later studies, in fields from clinical trials to genetics. Ioannidis asks how often we should expect this. If a paper reports a statistically significant result, what is the chance the relationship it claims really exists?
primer.quote: There is increasing concern that most current published research findings are false.

primer.heading: What they did
primer.body: Instead of running experiments, the paper does careful bookkeeping. Picture every relationship a field tests. Some are really true and most are not. Each test either 'finds' something or doesn't. Counting the four outcomes (real hits, false alarms, misses, correct nulls) gives the chance that a claimed finding is real. The paper then adds two distortions: bias, meaning results that get reported as findings when they shouldn't, and many teams testing the same question.

primer.heading: What they found
primer.body: The chance that a significant finding is true depends heavily on how plausible the idea was before the study. When a field tests thousands of long shots, almost every 'hit' is a false alarm. Low power, bias and crowds of competing teams push the odds down further. Only large, well-run studies of fairly plausible ideas give findings that are usually right.
primer.quote: Simulations show that for most study designs and settings, it is more likely for a research claim to be false than true.

primer.heading: Why it matters
primer.body: A p-value below 0.05 is not a stamp of truth. To judge a finding, you need to ask how likely it was beforehand, how big and well-powered the study was, how much room there was for bias, and how many others were testing the same thing. Keep the limits in mind: these are model calculations built on assumed inputs, not counts of real false papers.
primer.quote: Research is not most appropriately represented and summarized by p-values, but, unfortunately, there is a widespread notion that medical research articles should be interpreted based only on p-values.
primer.quote_where: Modeling the Framework for False Positive Findings

concepts.title: Significance has two failure modes
concepts.idea: When there is no real effect, about 5% of studies still cross p < 0.05; when there is a real effect, only a fraction of studies (the power) catch it.

predict.question: A lab runs 100 separate studies of a supplement that, unknown to them, does nothing at all. Each study is huge: 1,000 people per group. Roughly how many of the 100 studies will still score below 0.05?
options: Almost none, because huge studies don't make that mistake
About 50, because it's a coin flip with no effect
About 80, because big studies have high power
why: Right: with no real effect, the 0.05 line lets through about 5 false alarms in every 100 studies, whatever their size.
It feels as if size should protect you, but in the model the false-alarm share stayed near 5% even at 200 per group. Size only helps you catch real effects.
With no effect the p-values are spread evenly from 0 to 1, so only the slice below 0.05 counts: about 5%, not half.
Power is the catch rate for a real effect. Here there is nothing to catch, so power doesn't apply and only the 5% false-alarm rate is left.

terms.means: A study result whose p-value falls below the agreed line, usually 0.05
A significant result when there is really no effect
How often false positives happen when there is no effect. The 0.05 line sets it at about 5%
The share of studies that catch a real effect when one is there

model.title: 200 imaginary studies, each comparing two groups
model.note: Teaching model: each study compares two groups drawn from bell-shaped populations with the same spread, using a simple z-test. The true difference is measured in units of that spread. The 0.05 line is fixed, and there is no bias or flexible analysis. The long-run share is calculated for a two-sided test, and the simulated run of 200 studies wobbles around it by chance. Numbers are illustrative, not the paper's data.

controls.label: Size of the true difference (in spreads)

outputs.label: Catch rate if the difference is real
outputs.expr: normcdf(gap / sqrt(2 / n) - 1.96, 0, 1) + normcdf(-gap / sqrt(2 / n) - 1.96, 0, 1)

steps.say: Each dot is one imaginary study. It measures two groups of people and asks whether they differ. 200 studies run at once.
A dot's place is the study's p-value: how surprising its data would be if the groups were really the same. Below 0.05 counts as a result worth reporting.
This switch decides whether the groups truly differ, or are secretly identical.
This slider sets how big the true difference is.
And this one sets how many people each study measures per group.
These boxes count the share of studies that land below 0.05.

explore.prompt: Play with the switch and both sliders. Watch how the share of studies scoring below 0.05 behaves when nothing is there and when something is.

goals.text: Keep the true difference real and modest (smaller than 0.5 spreads), yet get studies to catch it at least 80% of the time.
hints: Two things make a real difference easier to catch: how big it is, and how many people each study has.
You may nudge the difference up a little, but it must stay modest. The people-per-group slider has to do most of the work.
With the difference near the top of its allowed range, you need roughly a hundred or more people per group.

goals.text: Switch the real difference off. Keep the studies big enough that they would catch the current difference more often than not if it were real. Does the long-run share drop below 5%?
hints: The catch-rate box still updates when the switch is off. It tells you what would happen if the difference were real.
Add people per group until that catch rate passes one half.
With the default difference you'll need well over fifty per group. Then compare the long-run share with what you saw at small sizes.

feedback.correct: Yes. With no real effect, about 5% of studies cross the 0.05 line by chance alone, and making studies bigger doesn't change that. So about 5 of the 100 supplement studies will be false alarms.
feedback.incorrect: It's tempting to think big studies can't produce false alarms, or that power matters here. But when nothing is there, the 0.05 line itself lets through about 5% of studies, whatever their size. Study size only changes how often a real effect is caught.

steps.say: Start with no real difference at all: both groups come from the same population. Small studies, 20 people per group.
Some dots still land below 0.05, about 5 in every 100. Such a study is called statistically significant. When nothing is really there, it's a false positive.
Make every study ten times bigger. The false-alarm share doesn't budge: still about 5%. This is the Type I error rate (α), and the 0.05 line itself sets it.
Now switch a real difference on: a small one, 0.3 spreads, back at 20 people per group. Only about 16 studies in 100 catch it.
The share of studies that catch a real effect is called power (1 − β). Here most studies miss an effect that is truly there.
Give each study 100 people per group. The catch rate climbs to about 56%.
At 200 per group it reaches about 85%. Two separate ways to go wrong: false alarms stay near 5% at any size, while misses shrink only as power grows.

understand.explanation: A study is called statistically significant when its p-value falls below 0.05. That line can fail in two different ways. When there is no real effect, about 5% of studies still cross it by chance. These false positives happen at the Type I error rate (α), and bigger studies don't reduce them. When there is a real effect, only some studies catch it: that share is the power (1 − β), and it grows with study size and effect size. The paper builds its whole argument on these two rates, taking α = 0.05 as the usual choice. This model assumes clean, honest analyses; real research can be messier.
understand.quote: The probability of a study finding a true relationship reflects the power 1 - β (one minus the Type II error rate). The probability of claiming a relationship when none truly exists reflects the Type I error rate, α.
understand.quote_where: Section 'It can be proven that most claimed research findings are false'

equation.text: ;  share significant = α ≈ 0.05 when it is not

connect.caption: The paper calls the catch rate for a real relationship the power, 1 − β (the 'Catch rate if the difference is real' box). It calls the false-alarm rate α, usually 0.05. The model computes power from a simple z-test formula; the paper uses the two rates directly.

concepts.recap: Significance can fail twice: about 5% false alarms when nothing is there, and missed effects whenever power is low.

concepts.title: How likely was it before you looked?
concepts.idea: The chance that a significant finding is true depends on the ratio of true to false ideas being tested: when real effects are rare, false alarms outnumber real hits.

predict.question: A genome scan tests 100,000 gene variants. About 10 are truly linked to a disease, so there is roughly 1 true idea for every 10,000 false ones. The study has 60% power at the usual 5% cut-off, with no bias. A variant comes out just significant. Roughly how likely is it to be real?
why: Tempting because p < 0.05 sounds like '95% sure'. But the 5% is the false-alarm rate among false ideas, not the chance a claim is real. With almost 100,000 false ideas, that 5% makes thousands of false alarms.
Power tells you how often a real effect gets caught. It does not tell you how many of the claims are real. The handful of real hits is buried under the false alarms.
Fifty-fifty needs real hits and false alarms to be about equal. At 80% power that only happens near 16 false ideas per true one, and this field is about 10,000 to 1.
Correct. About 6 real hits (60% of 10) sit against about 5,000 false alarms (5% of ~100,000). The paper works this case in Box 1 and gets about 12 in 10,000, roughly 0.12%.

terms.means: How many true ideas a field tests for each false one, before any study is run
The share of significant, claimed findings that are actually real

model.title: 1000 tested ideas, sorted by whether they are real and whether the study came out significant
model.note: Teaching model: a field tests 1000 ideas, each once, with power fixed at 80%, the significance cut-off fixed at 5%, and no bias. The table shows expected counts, not one random run. The formula is the paper's, but the counts are illustrative, not the paper's data.

controls.label: False ideas tested for each true one

outputs.label: Share of claimed findings that are real

steps.say: This grid sorts 1000 ideas a field tests. The columns say whether an idea is truly real. The rows say whether its study came out significant.
The top row is what gets claimed: real hits on the left, false alarms on the right.
Every study here has 80% power and uses the usual 5% cut-off. Those two stay fixed.
This slider sets how many false ideas the field tests for each true one. Watch the top row as it moves.
This number is the share of claimed findings that are actually real.

explore.prompt: Slide through fields from 'half the ideas are true' to 'true ideas are rare' and watch the claimed-findings row tip over.

goals.text: Find the most lopsided field, with at least 14 false ideas per true one, where a claimed finding is still more likely real than not.
hints: Watch the two cells in the top row as you move the slider. Which way does the balance tip?
You want the point just before false alarms overtake real hits, where the two cells are almost equal.
Each true idea gives 0.8 of a real hit. Each false idea gives 0.05 of a false alarm. How many false ideas does it take to match one true idea's hits? Stop one short of that.

goals.text: Make false alarms outnumber real hits about three to one.
hints: Compare the two top-row cells as a ratio, not as separate numbers.
That ratio grows in step with the slider. Double the false ideas per true one and the ratio doubles.
In the first goal you found where the ratio is about 1 to 1. A field three times more lopsided gives 3 to 1.

feedback.correct: Right. At about 10,000 false ideas per true one, the 5% false-alarm rate produces thousands of false alarms, while 60% of 10 real variants gives about 6 real hits. A barely significant result is still very unlikely to be real. The paper's Box 1 puts it at about 12 in 10,000.
feedback.incorrect: You may have read p < 0.05 or the power as the chance a claim is real. Neither is. What matters is how real hits compare with false alarms, and when true ideas are extremely rare, the false alarms swamp the hits.

steps.say: Start with a field where half the ideas are true: 1 false idea for each true one. That is 500 real ideas, and 80% of them are caught: 400 real hits. Of the 500 false ideas, 5% slip through: 25 false alarms.
The balance of true to false ideas, judged before any study is run, is called the pre-study odds (R). Here R = 1. The slider shows its flip side, false ideas per true one, so R = 1 ÷ slider.
Of the 425 claimed findings, 400 are real, about 94%. This share is called the positive predictive value (PPV).
Now make true ideas rarer: 10 false per true one, so R = 1/10. Real ideas drop to about 91, and real hits to about 73. False alarms rise to about 45.
PPV falls to about 62%. Nothing about the studies changed. Only the mix of ideas going in did.
At 50 false per true, about 16 real hits face about 49 false alarms. The false-alarm cell lights up: it has overtaken the hits. PPV is about 24%.
Notice that false alarms can never top 50, which is 5% of 1000. They barely grow. What changes is that the real hits shrink toward nothing.
At 200 false per true, about 4 real hits sit against about 50 false alarms. PPV is about 7%: a significant result here is far more likely a false alarm than a discovery.

understand.explanation: A significant result can come from a real effect (a real hit) or from a false idea that got lucky (a false alarm). How many of each you get depends on the mix of ideas being tested, the pre-study odds (R). When true ideas are common, real hits dominate. When they are rare, the steady 5% of false ideas that slip through outnumbers the few real hits, even though every study is run perfectly. Ioannidis puts this into a 2 × 2 table of expected counts and derives the positive predictive value (PPV) = (1 − β)R/(R − βR + α), so a finding is more likely true than false only when power × R exceeds α. In his genome example (Box 1), R is about 1 in 10,000 and a just-significant result is real only about 12 times in 10,000. This assumes no bias and one study per idea, and in practice R is never known exactly: the paper says it must be estimated with rough, partly subjective assumptions.
understand.quote: According to the 2 × 2 table, one gets PPV = (1 - β)R/(R - βR + α). A research finding is thus more likely true than false if (1 - β)R > α.
understand.quote_where: Modeling the Framework for False Positive Findings

check.task: Put the model in a state where only about 1 in 10 claimed findings is real (between 8% and 12%).
check.hint: One real claim in ten means about 9 false alarms for every real hit. False alarms level off near 50, so real hits must shrink to around 5 or 6. How rare must true ideas be for that?
check.misconception: That a result with p < 0.05 is real about 95% of the time, whatever field it comes from.

connect.caption: PPV (orange) is the share of claimed findings that are real. R is the pre-study odds of true to false ideas, the inverse of the slider (R = 1 ÷ false ideas per true one). 1 − β is power, fixed here at 0.8, and α is the significance cut-off, fixed at 0.05. This is the paper's formula for one unbiased study per idea.

concepts.recap: A significant result is only as trustworthy as the field it comes from: when true ideas are rare, false alarms outnumber real hits and most claimed findings are false.

concepts.title: Small studies, small effects, weaker findings
concepts.idea: Lower power shrinks the number of real hits while the false alarms stay the same, so findings from small studies or small effects are less likely to be true.

predict.question: Two labs test the same kind of idea in the same field. Lab A studies 50 people and Lab B studies 5,000. Both report a result just under p < 0.05. Whose finding is more likely to be real?
options: Lab B's: its big study catches real effects far more often, so real hits make up more of its significant results
Equal: both crossed the same p < 0.05 line
Lab A's: getting significance with only 50 people shows the effect must be strong
Lab B's, because big studies produce fewer false alarms
why: Right. Same field means the same odds, and the false-alarm cell is the same for both. The big study fills the real-hit cell much more, so its PPV is higher.
Tempting, because the p-value line is identical. But the share of significant results that are real also depends on how often the study catches real effects, and that is much lower for 50 people.
It feels like an achievement, but a small study gets significant results from false ideas just as often (about 5%). It catches far fewer real ones, so its hits are more likely to be false alarms.
Right lab, wrong reason. The false-alarm rate is set by the 5% cut-off, whatever the study size. Big studies win by adding real hits, not by removing false alarms.

terms.means: The chance that a study comes out significant when the effect it tests is real. Small studies have low power.
How big a real effect is. Small effects are harder to detect, so they also lower power.

model.title: 1000 tested ideas, sorted by whether they are real and whether the study came out significant
model.note: Teaching model: a field tests 1000 ideas, each once, with the significance cut-off fixed at 5% and no bias. The new slider sets how often a study catches a real effect, which stands in for both study size and how big the real effects are. The table shows expected counts, not one random run. The formula is the paper's no-bias case, but the counts are illustrative, not the paper's data.

Chance a study catches a real effect

steps.say: It's the same table as before: 1000 tested ideas, split by whether they are real and whether the study came out significant.
This slider is the same one as before. It sets how many false ideas the field tests for each real one.
This slider is new. It sets how often a study catches a real effect when there is one. Watch the real hits shrink as it drops.

explore.prompt: Now you set the field. Use both sliders to see when weak studies sink a field, and when strong studies can rescue one.

goals.text: In a field where at least 1 in 5 tested ideas is real, make most claimed findings false.
hints: Making real ideas rarer only goes so far here. What else can shrink the real hits?
Keep the field fairly well aimed, then pull the catch-rate slider a long way down.
Most findings are false once real hits fall below false alarms. Use as many false ideas as the goal allows, then try the lowest few catch rates.

goals.text: In a field where real ideas are 1 in 18 or rarer, make real hits outnumber false alarms.
hints: Rarer real ideas mean more false alarms, and you can't remove those. What can you do about the real hits?
Make the field just as rare as the goal allows, then push the catch rate up.
The margin is thin: only the top few catch-rate settings work, and only at the least rare end of the allowed range.

feedback.correct: Yes. Within one field the false alarms are fixed by the 5% cut-off. The bigger study catches more of the real effects, so a larger share of its significant results are real.
feedback.incorrect: You may have treated p < 0.05 as meaning the same thing in every study, or assumed big studies cut false alarms. The cut-off sets the false alarms. Study size changes how many real hits sit beside them, and that is what changes the share that are real.

steps.say: Let's aim the field less well: 10 false ideas for each real one. With studies that catch real effects 80% of the time, we get about 73 real hits against 45 false alarms. 62% of claimed findings are real.
The chance that a study catches a real effect is called its power. Small studies have low power: with few people, real effects often fail to reach significance.
Cut the power to 50%. Real hits fall to about 45. Now look at the false alarms: still 45.
Why don't false alarms move? They come from ideas that aren't real. For those, only the 5% cut-off matters, not how big the study is.
Drop power to 20%, like a small study. Only 18 real hits are left beside 45 false alarms. The missed real ideas pile up below, and just 29% of findings are real.
Small effects do the same thing. When the real effect size is small, even a decent study often misses it. Small effects lower power just as small samples do.

Push power down to 5%, the same rate as the false alarms. Real ideas and false ones now reach significance equally often. The share of real findings, 9%, equals the share of tested ideas that were real. The study told you nothing new.

understand.explanation: A significant result comes from one of two cells: real hits or false alarms. Power only touches the real-hit cell. Lower it and real hits shrink, while false alarms stay fixed by the 5% cut-off, so a growing share of claimed findings are false. Small studies and small effects both lower power, so both make findings less trustworthy. As power sinks towards 5%, a significant result adds almost nothing to what you knew before. The paper shows this from its PPV formula rather than by counting real studies. It contrasts large cardiology trials with molecular studies about 100 times smaller, and smoking's large effects (relative risks 3–20) with tiny genetic ones (1.1–1.5), all with other factors held equal and bias set aside.
understand.quote: The smaller the studies conducted in a scientific field, the less likely the research findings are to be true. Small sample size means smaller power and, for all functions above, the PPV for a true research finding decreases as power decreases towards 1 − β = 0.05.

connect.caption: This is the paper's no-bias formula. (1 − β) is power, the new green slider. R is the pre-study odds, which equals 1 divided by the false ideas tested per true one. α is the 5% cut-off, held fixed. Lowering (1 − β) shrinks the top of the fraction, which is the real hits. The α part of the bottom is the false alarms, and it doesn't change, so PPV falls.

concepts.recap: Small studies and small effects lower power: real hits shrink, false alarms don't, so significant findings are less likely to be true.

activities.prompt: Same field, same odds (5 false ideas tested for each real one). The only difference is study size. On the left is a large, cardiology-style trial; on the right is a small study. Compare the two significant-result cells.
activities.takeaway: False alarms are about 42 in both. The large trial has about 150 real hits beside them, so 78% of its findings are real. The small study has about 33, which gives 44%. Same field, same cut-off: only power changed. In the paper, cardiology trials and small molecular studies also differ in other ways, but holding the odds fixed isolates the role of power.

activities.question: Two fields run studies of the same size, and in both about 1 in 10 tested ideas is real. In field A the real effects are large, like smoking's effect on lung cancer (the paper cites relative risks of 3–20). In field B they are tiny, like single gene variants for complex diseases (1.1–1.5). Which field's significant findings are more likely to be true?

options.text: Field A: large effects are easier to catch, so its studies have more power and more real hits beside the same false alarms
options.feedback: Right. Effect size feeds into power. With the same study size and the same odds, field A's real-hit cell is bigger, so its PPV is higher. This is the paper's Corollary 2.

options.text: Field B: hunting tiny effects takes more care, so its findings are more trustworthy
options.feedback: Care is a separate matter. With the same study size, tiny effects are missed more often, so field B has fewer real hits beside the same number of false alarms.

options.text: Neither: same study size and same odds give the same share of true findings
options.feedback: Study size isn't the only thing that sets power. Effect size does too, so the two fields have different power and different PPV.

options.text: You can't tell without seeing each study's p-value
options.feedback: The p-values would show whether each study crossed 0.05, but the question is what crossing means. That depends on power and odds, and power is lower in field B.

hints: Which cell of the table does effect size change: real hits or false alarms?
A tiny real effect is easy to miss. What does that do to power?

concepts.title: Bias turns non-findings into findings
concepts.idea: If a share u of analyses that should have come out null get reported as findings anyway, the extra 'hits' come mostly from false ideas, so PPV drops.

predict.question: Imagine a field of tiny studies where power is only 5%, so a real effect is caught no more often than a false idea crosses the cut-off. What does adding bias do to the share of claimed findings that are real?
options: It drops sharply, as it does in other fields
It stays where it started, at the share of tested ideas that are real
It rises, because bias also rescues real ideas that were missed
why: Tempting, since bias lowered PPV every time so far. That was because the nulls were mostly false ideas. At 5% power, real and false ideas both come out null 95% of the time, so bias draws on both equally.

Right. When power equals the 5% false-alarm rate, real and false ideas are claimed at the same rate, with or without bias. So PPV stays at the starting share. This is the paper's exception: 'unless 1 − β ≤ α'.
Bias does rescue some missed real ideas. But it rescues false ones in exactly the same proportion, so the share can't rise. Try it: set power to its minimum and move the new slider.

terms.means: In the paper's sense, the share u of analyses that should have come out not significant but get reported as findings anyway, through choices in design, data, analysis or reporting
PPV: the share of claimed findings that are actually real
Writing up only the analyses or outcomes that came out significant
Publicly fixing a study's plan before the data come in, so the analysis can't be reshaped afterwards

The new slider is the paper's u: a share of the analyses that should have come out null get reported as findings anyway. Following the paper's assumption, this share is the same for real and not-real ideas. The table shows expected counts, not one random run. The formula is the paper's Table 2 case, but the counts are illustrative, not the paper's data.

steps.say: Same table as before: 1000 tested ideas, split by whether they are real and whether they end up claimed as findings. The top row is what gets published as a discovery.

One new slider. Of the studies that came out null, what share still get written up as findings? This could happen through a tweak to the analysis or a choice of what to report. The new second row counts these.
Watch the claimed row swell, and watch the share of claimed findings that are real.

explore.prompt: Bias acts only on null results. Use that to predict where it does the most damage, then test your guess on the table.

goals.text: Keep studies well powered (at least 80%) and the field fairly focused (at most five false ideas per true one), yet make false alarms outnumber real hits in the claimed row.
hints: Without the new slider, can false alarms ever win under these limits? Check the claimed row.
The new slider takes a share of each column's null results. Which column has more null results to feed it, and how can you make that column bigger?
Take the false-ideas slider up to its allowed limit first. Then raise the new slider one step at a time until the right-hand claimed cell turns larger.

goals.text: Find a field where a modest amount of bias (at most 15%) cuts the share of claimed findings that are real to less than half of what it would be with no bias.
goals.when: bias > 0 && bias <= 15 && ppv < 0.5 * ((power / 100) * true_ideas / ((power / 100) * true_ideas + 0.05 * (1000 - true_ideas)))
hints: Bias hurts most where real ideas are rare.
Note the share with no bias first, then add a little and compare. In the focused field from the walkthrough, a small dose barely dents it.
Push the false-ideas slider well past twenty before adding any bias. With dozens of false ideas per true one, a small step on the new slider is enough.

feedback.correct: Yes. Bias hurts because null results are mostly false ideas. When power is as low as the false-alarm rate, real and false ideas come out null equally often. Bias then pads both columns in the same proportion, and PPV stays at the starting share of real ideas.
feedback.incorrect: You probably expected bias always to lower PPV, or to help by rescuing missed real ideas. What matters is the mix of the null results it draws on. At 5% power that mix matches the mix of ideas tested, so PPV doesn't move. It only falls when the nulls are mostly false ideas, which is the usual case.

steps.say: Start with an honest field: one false idea for each true one, 80% power, and no null result reported as a finding. 400 real hits against 25 false alarms, so 94% of claims are real.

Look at the 'Not claimed' row. These are the null results. Only 100 sit under 'Truly real' (the missed ideas). 475 sit under 'Not real'. Real ideas are usually caught, but false ideas almost always come out null.
Now let 10% of null results be reported as findings anyway. The paper calls this share bias, u. It takes 10% of each column's nulls: about 10 extra real hits, but about 48 extra false alarms.

The share of claimed findings that are real is called the positive predictive value, PPV. It drops from 94% to 85%. The paper's estimate for a well-run, adequately powered trial with a 50% starting chance is about 85%.
Push u to 30%. The real column gains 30 more claims, while the not-real column gains about 143. PPV falls to 72%.
Now switch to a long-shot field: 20 false ideas for each true one, and no bias. PPV is already only 44%, with about 38 real hits and 48 false alarms.
Give it the same 30% bias. Real hits barely move, from 38 to 41, because there are hardly any real nulls to draw from. False alarms jump from 48 to about 319. PPV crashes to 11%.

understand.explanation: The paper defines bias as anything in design, data, analysis or reporting that turns a result that should have been null into a reported finding; selective reporting is a typical form. Bias works on null results, and null results are mostly false ideas: a real idea is usually caught, but a false idea almost always comes out null. So each step up in u adds a few real hits and many false alarms, and PPV falls fastest where true ideas are rare. In the paper's schizophrenia gene example (Box 1), u = 0.10 cuts the chance that a significant finding is true from about 12 × 10⁻⁴ to 4.4 × 10⁻⁴. The paper suggests common standards and study registration as remedies, but warns that bias remains a major problem even in strict designs. Like the paper, the model assumes u is the same for real and false ideas; the paper also notes that 'reverse bias' can bury real findings, though it judges this less common.
understand.quote: Thus, with increasing bias, the chances that a research finding is true diminish considerably.

connect.caption: The paper's formula for PPV with bias. 1 − β is the power slider. R is the ratio of true to false ideas, so R = 1 ÷ (false ideas per true one). u is the new slider, and α = 0.05. On top, uβR is bias rescuing missed real ideas. Below, u − uα is bias rescuing the far larger pool of false ideas' nulls.

concepts.recap: Bias feeds on null results, and null results are mostly false ideas, so every bit of bias adds far more false alarms than real hits.

activities.title: What moves u?
activities.prompt: Each card is a research practice the paper discusses. Does it tend to raise bias (more null results turned into findings) or lower it?

cards.text: Running subgroup analyses that weren't planned, after seeing the data
cards.feedback: The paper lists post hoc subgroup analyses as one way to push results across p = 0.05. Every extra unplanned cut is another chance for a null to become a 'finding'.

cards.text: Deciding after the fact to include or exclude certain patients
cards.feedback: The paper names 'serendipitous inclusion or exclusion of certain patients or controls' as a form of manipulation that raises u.

cards.text: Changing the disease definition until a result crosses p < 0.05
cards.feedback: Changes in disease or control definitions give more ways to turn a null into a positive. The paper's Corollary 4 calls this flexibility.

cards.text: Writing up only the outcomes that came out significant
cards.feedback: Selective reporting is the paper's 'typical form' of bias. The paper notes strong evidence that it happens even in randomized trials.

cards.text: Registering the study plan before collecting data
cards.feedback: The paper suggests upfront registration, at least for randomized trials, and adhering to a protocol. A fixed plan leaves less room to reshape a null afterwards.

cards.text: Following common standards for how trials are run and reported
cards.feedback: Corollary 4: adherence to common standards 'is likely to increase the proportion of true findings'.

cards.text: Using an outcome everyone agrees on, like death
cards.feedback: The paper contrasts unequivocal outcomes such as death with many made-up scales. Fewer outcome choices mean fewer ways to manufacture a finding.

cards.text: Using a standard, agreed analysis method instead of trying many and reporting the 'best'
cards.feedback: The paper says fields with stereotyped methods, such as the log-rank test, may yield more true findings than fields where only 'best' results are reported.

activities.takeaway: Flexibility after the data arrive raises u. Fixing choices in advance lowers it. The paper warns that even strict designs still show substantial bias.

concepts.title: The hotter the field, the shakier the finding
concepts.idea: When n teams test the same question and attention goes to whichever one gets a significant result, the chance of at least one false alarm grows quickly, so that lone finding is less likely to be true.

predict.question: A dozen labs test whether a popular supplement improves memory. One gets p < 0.05 and publishes; eleven shelve null results. Compared with one lab's significant result on a question nobody else studied (same study size, same prior odds), how should you rate the published finding?
options: More likely real: a popular question attracts good researchers
About as likely real: each lab's study is just as good
Less likely real: twelve chances for a fluke stand behind it
Certainly false: eleven labs found nothing
why: Popularity feels like a sign of quality, but the studies are the same size. Twelve teams give a not-real idea twelve chances at a fluke, and only the lucky one got noticed.
Each study is equally good, but we only see the one that crossed p < 0.05. Picking the winner from twelve tries inflates false alarms, so it is weaker evidence than a lone study.
Right. With twelve teams, about 46% of not-real ideas get at least one significant result (1 − 0.95¹²). Real hits can't grow past the power, so the finding sits near the prior odds.
Less likely real is not the same as certainly false. Small studies often miss real effects, so one positive and eleven nulls could still hide a real effect. Weigh all twelve results together.

terms.means: The share of claimed findings that are actually real: the chance a significant result is true
The chance an idea is real before anyone tests it, set by how many false ideas are tested for each true one

model.title: 1000 tested ideas, each tested by several teams, sorted by whether they are real and whether any team came out significant
model.note: Teaching model: a field tests 1000 ideas. Each idea is tested by the same number of independent teams with equal power. An idea counts as a claimed finding if at least one team gets p < 0.05, and the other teams' results are ignored. The significance cut-off is fixed at 5% and there is no bias. The counts follow the paper's formula for several independent studies (no-bias case) and are expected counts, not one random run. The slider can't reach the paper's genome odds of about 1 real idea in 10,000, so this is an illustrative miniature, not the paper's data.

controls.label: False ideas tested for each true one
Chance a study catches a real effect

outputs.label: Chance an idea is real before testing
Real hits (real, at least one team significant)
False alarms (not real, at least one team significant)
Share of claimed findings that are real

rows.label: At least one team significant (claimed finding)

steps.say: Same table as before: 1000 tested ideas, sorted by whether they're real and whether they came out significant.
New slider: how many separate teams test each idea. An idea now counts as a claimed finding if at least one team gets a significant result. The other teams are ignored.
Two new boxes. One shows the chance an idea was real before anyone tested it. The other shows how many times likelier it looks after a claimed finding.

explore.prompt: Real ideas are rare in this field, and teams keep piling onto each question. See how far you can push the number of teams before a lone finding stops being convincing.

goals.text: In a field where under 1% of tested ideas are real, find the most teams per idea you can have while a claimed finding is still at least 5 times likelier to be real than before testing.
hints: Every added team adds more chances of a fluke. The only lever working the other way is how reliable each study is.
First make real ideas rare. Then max out the chance a study catches a real effect, add teams one at a time and watch the 'times likelier' box.
The answer is a small single-digit number of teams. One team past it, even near-perfect studies can't reach 5×.

feedback.correct: Yes. Twelve teams means twelve chances for a not-real idea to produce a fluke, and the shelved nulls hide how much testing happened. Real effects can't be caught much more often than the power already allows. So the lone published result is weaker evidence than a single isolated study.
feedback.incorrect: The trap is judging the published study on its own merits. The other eleven labs are invisible, but they still count: each one was another 5% chance of a false alarm. Picking the one significant result out of twelve inflates the false alarms far more than the real hits. The finding is less likely real, though not certainly false.

steps.say: Let's build the paper's genome example in miniature. In the paper, real links are very rare, and each study has 60% power. Our slider stops at 200 false ideas per true one, so here only about 1 idea in 201 is real.
Before anyone tests, the chance any given idea is real is just 0.5%. Call this the pre-study probability.
One team per idea: about 3 real hits against about 50 false alarms. So a claimed finding is real only about 5.7% of the time. That share is the positive predictive value (PPV).
Still, 5.7% is about 11 times the 0.5% we started with. That is close to the 12-fold boost the paper reports for one study. A significant result taught us something.
Now two teams test every idea, and attention goes to whichever gets significance. False alarms nearly double, to about 97. Each team is a fresh 5% chance of a fluke.
Five teams. Real hits creep only from 3 to about 5: they were already likely to be caught, and there are only 5 real ideas to find. False alarms have climbed past 200.
Ten teams. About 40% of the not-real ideas now get at least one significant result. A lone finding is real only about 1.2% of the time, roughly 2.5 times the starting 0.5%.

The paper's genome numbers are starker. With no bias, ten teams test the same genes and one finds a significant link. The paper puts the chance it's real at 1.5 in 10,000, against 1 in 10,000 before. Research barely moved us.

understand.explanation: When many teams test the same question, each team is another 5% chance that a not-real idea throws up a fluke. So the share of false ideas with at least one significant result grows as 1 − 0.95ⁿ, about 40% with ten teams. Real effects were already caught at the rate set by power, so real hits can barely grow. If attention goes to the one significant team, the positive predictive value (PPV) of that lone finding sinks back toward the pre-study probability. The paper derives this from its 2 × 2 table for n independent studies of equal power, and shows it in its figures and in the genome example: 1.5 × 10⁻⁴ after ten teams, against 10⁻⁴ before. The paper also notes that hot fields can sometimes bring larger studies and better standards, and its remedy is to weigh the totality of the evidence, including the teams that found nothing.
understand.quote: Corollary 6: The hotter a scientific field (with more scientific teams involved), the less likely the research findings are to be true. This seemingly paradoxical corollary follows because, as stated above, the PPV of isolated findings decreases when many teams of investigators are involved in the same field.

check.task: Put the model in a state where one team's significant result would be more likely real than not, but with several teams racing, the lone claimed finding is more likely false than real.
check.hint: First find a field where real ideas are uncommon but not rare, so that with one team the claimed findings are still mostly real. Then raise the number of teams and watch the share that is real.
check.misconception: That more teams testing a question can only add confirmation, so the finding gets more trustworthy. When only the one significant result gets attention, every extra team is another chance of a false alarm.

connect.caption: This is the paper's formula for n independent studies of equal power, without bias. PPV is the share of claimed findings that are real. R is the ratio of true to false ideas: 1 divided by the 'false ideas for each true one' slider. β is the chance one study misses a real effect, so 1 − β is the power slider. n is the number of teams. α = 0.05 is the significance cut-off. [1 − α]ⁿ is the chance no team gets a fluke on a false idea, so 1 − [1 − α]ⁿ is the false-alarm rate that climbs with n.

concepts.recap: When many teams chase one question and only the significant result gets noticed, false alarms grow with every team while real hits can't, so the lone finding barely beats the prior odds.
